title: If Trump took responsibility for coronavirus missteps, it might actually help him.
citation: David Ryan Miller, Andrew Reeves. (2020). "If Trump took responsibility for coronavirus missteps, it might actually help him.."
card_summary: Survey experiments show that politicians who claim responsibility for crises receive higher public approval than those who deflect blame.
plain_english_summary: When politicians admit mistakes during a crisis instead of blaming others, people tend to view them more favorably, as shown by several survey experiments.
research_question: Which strategy is most effective for political leaders during a crisis: avoiding blame or taking responsibility?
research_highlights: Claiming blame is the most effective strategy for leaders to maintain or increase public approval during crises.
Leaders who accept responsibility for mistakes receive much higher approval ratings than those who deflect blame.
This effect was observed in both real-world and hypothetical crisis scenarios across multiple survey experiments.
methods: Survey experiments using both real-world and hypothetical crisis scenarios.
Online convenience samples (Amazon Mechanical Turk) and a nationally representative panel (The American Panel Survey).
data_sources: Amazon Mechanical Turk online convenience samples
key_variables: Leader's blame strategy (claiming blame, deflecting blame, blame-neutral)
Likelihood to vote for the official
time_period: March 2016 (Flint water crisis study); 2011-2018 (TAPS panel); other studies not precisely dated
pull_quote: In a crisis, avoiding blame is not the best way to maintain public support. Truman, not Machiavelli, offers leaders the better approach for turbulent times like the present.
